1. "The person who eats cauliflower is not the same as the person who watches martial-arts." => Cauliflower != martial-arts (different persons).

So cabbage must be at same position? No same person can't have both cabbage and juice because each person has unique values per attribute, but could be same person? But each person has one food and one beverage, so they could be same person (cabbage eater also drinks juice) - that would be position equal, which is not left. However the phrase "not anywhere to the left of" might imply "not to the left of" meaning cannot be left, but could be same position or right. Usually in such puzzles, "not anywhere to the left of" means "not left of", i.e., position(cabbage) >= position(juice). Since same person can't have both cabbage and juice (different categories) but could be same person if they have both cabbage food and juice beverage. That's allowed. So constraint: position(cabbage) >= position(juice). (i.e., cabbage is at same position or to the right of juice.)

3. "The person who watches fantasy and the person who drinks water have different parity positions." => parity(fantasy) != parity(water). Parity: odd/even positions. Positions 1 (odd), 2 (even), 3 (odd). So parity difference means one is odd, other even. So fantasy and water are on opposite parity.

4. "The person who plays parkour is not anywhere to the right of the person who watches fantasy." => parkour position <= fantasy position (cannot be right of). So parkour is left of or same position as fantasy. Since each person has unique sport and movie-genre, they could be same person? Could a person both play parkour and watch fantasy? Yes, a person can have sport= parkour and movie-genre= fantasy. The constraint says "not anywhere to the right of" meaning parkour is not strictly to the right; could be same position (i.e., same person) or left. So position(parkour) <= position(fantasy).

5. "The person who plays rugby and the person who drinks water have different parity positions." => parity(rugby) != parity(water).

6. "The person who eats cauliflower and the person who likes filmmaking have the same parity positions." => parity(cauliflower) == parity(filmmaking).

7. "Either the person who eats strawberry is the same as the person who watches action or the person who watches action is the same as the person who plays rugby, but not both." => XOR: (strawberry = action) XOR (action = rugby). So exactly one of those equalities holds. Note "same as" means same person. So either strawberry eater is the action watcher (and action watcher is not rugby player) OR action watcher is rugby player (and strawberry eater is not action watcher). But not both. So we have two possibilities.

8. "The person who likes baking and the person who plays parkour have different parity positions." => parity(baking) != parity(parkour).

9. "The person who likes baking is the same as the person who plays parkour or the person who likes baking is the same as the person who watches fantasy or both." => baking = parkour OR baking = fantasy (or both). So baking person is either parkour person, fantasy watcher, or both (i.e., same person has baking hobby and also sport parkour and/or movie fantasy). Since each person has one hobby, one sport, one movie-genre. So "baking = parkour" means the person whose hobby is baking also has sport parkour. "baking = fantasy" means the person whose hobby is baking also has movie-genre fantasy. Both could be true if that person has hobby baking, sport parkour, and movie-genre fantasy (i.e., all three attributes on same person). That is allowed.

10. "The person who drinks 7up is not anywhere to the right of the person who watches action." => position(7up) <= position(action). (cannot be right of). Could be same person (if same person drinks 7up and watches action) - that would satisfy <=.

Also we have uniqueness constraints: each attribute value used exactly once per category.
